items.topic: Mata v. Avianca: using AI for research without fake facts
items.hook: In 2023, two New York lawyers filed a brief citing court cases that didn't exist.
items.body: How to use AI for research without becoming the next cautionary tale.
parts:
In 2023, two New York lawyers filed a brief citing six court cases that didn't exist. ChatGPT had invented them, quotes and all.

Here's how to use AI for research without becoming the next cautionary tale:

The case was Mata v. Avianca. In June 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel fined the lawyers and their firm $5,000.

The bigger cost: their names became the standard example of what not to do.

Why it happens: a chatbot predicts plausible text. A case citation is just a pattern: names, volume, court, year.

A model can produce a perfect-looking pattern with nothing behind it.

Rule 1: Use AI for structure, not facts.

Outlines, first drafts, counterarguments, questions you forgot to ask. Those stay useful even when they're imperfect.

Rule 2: Every fact that leaves your desk gets checked against a primary source.

Not a second chatbot. The court record, the study, the filing.

Rule 3: Ask the tool where a claim came from.

If it can't point to a source you can open and read, treat the claim as a draft, not a fact.

The takeaway: AI makes you faster at producing words. It doesn't make any of them true.

Your name is still on the work.
items.cta: Bookmark this for the next time a chatbot sounds very sure of itself.

items.hook: Before your next big decision, assume it already failed.
items.body:
That's the premortem, a technique psychologist Gary Klein described in Harvard Business Review in 2007.

How it works: before a project starts, the team imagines it's a year later and the project has failed badly. Everyone takes a few minutes to write down why. Then you go around the room and fix the biggest risks while they're still cheap.

Why it beats the usual "any concerns?" question: asking for concerns invites polite silence. Declaring failure as a fact gives people permission to name what they already suspect.

Klein cites 1989 research by Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington: imagining that an outcome has already happened increased people's ability to correctly identify reasons for it by 30%.

Try it this week:
1. Pick one decision with real stakes.
2. Write: "It's six months from now. This failed. Why?"
3. List five reasons in five minutes.
4. Fix the top two before you start.

items.topic: Which jobs to hand AI and which to keep
items.hook: 5 jobs to hand AI this week, and 3 to keep for yourself.
items.body: Most people try AI like a search engine, get a confident wrong answer, and decide it's overrated. It's much better at some jobs than others. Here's the split worth using.
parts: Hand off: first drafts. A rough version in 30 seconds beats a blank page. It types; you edit.
Hand off: summaries of long documents and meeting notes. Ask for decisions, owners and deadlines, then skim the original once.
Hand off: counterarguments. Ask "What would a smart skeptic say about this plan?" It's quick at finding holes you're too close to see.
Hand off: reformatting. Notes to email, email to bullet points, bullet points to a slide outline.
Hand off: spreadsheet formulas. Describe what you want in plain English, then test the formula on a few rows you can check by hand.
Keep: facts that go out under your name. Models can state false things fluently. Verify against the source.
Keep: judgment calls about people. Hiring, feedback, hard conversations. AI can help you prepare; the decision is yours.
Keep: anything confidential your company hasn't approved for AI tools. Check the policy before you paste.
items.cta: Which of the five would save you the most time this week?

items.hook: Most couples aren't really fighting about money. They're fighting about what money means.
items.body:
Relationship researcher John Gottman found that about 69% of conflicts between couples are "perpetual": they come from lasting differences in personality or values, and they never fully go away.

Money is a classic one. For one person, a full savings account means safety. For the other, money sitting there is life not being lived. Neither is wrong. They're running different scripts.

Couples who do well don't erase those differences. They manage them, with less heat and more structure. A few structures that help:

• A monthly money date. Same day, 30 minutes, no surprises saved up for it.
• A yours/mine/ours split: shared bills from a joint account, plus personal money nobody has to justify.
• A spending number that triggers a talk first. Pick it together, before you need it.

The goal isn't agreeing on everything. It's having the same argument less often.
items.cta: What's one money habit you and your partner see differently?

items.hook: The cheapest health habit there is takes 2 minutes and needs no gym.
items.body:
A 2022 review in the journal Sports Medicine pooled seven studies and found that light walking after a meal, even for 2–5 minutes, lowered blood sugar and insulin compared with sitting. Standing helped blood sugar a little; walking helped more.

No equipment. No membership. Stand up after you eat and move.

General information, not medical advice. If you manage blood sugar for a health condition, ask your doctor what's right for you.
parts: A 2-minute habit with real research behind it.
After a meal, your blood sugar rises, then falls.
A 2022 review of 7 studies (Sports Medicine) found light walking after eating, even 2–5 minutes, lowered blood sugar and insulin compared with sitting.
Standing up helped blood sugar a little. Walking helped more.
Timing: the authors suggest moving within 60–90 minutes after eating.
Make it automatic: walk to the mailbox and back after dinner, take calls on your feet, do the dishes before you sit down.
Small habit, compounding return. Save this for after your next meal.
items.cta: Save this and try it after dinner tonight.

items.topic: Bitcoin Pizza Day: 10,000 BTC for two pizzas
titles: He Paid 10,000 Bitcoin for Two Pizzas
The Most Expensive Lunch in History
items.hook: In 2010, a man paid for two pizzas with money that would later be worth a billion dollars.
items.caption: May 22, 2010: 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas. Worth about $41 then. Worth $1 billion once bitcoin crossed $100,000. Not investment advice, just the most expensive lunch in history.
items.cta: Follow for true money stories with a lesson inside.

items.topic: Save More Tomorrow: committing future raises to savings
titles: The Savings Plan You Never Feel
How to Save 4x More Without a Smaller Paycheck
items.hook: Two economists got people saving almost four times more, without cutting anything today.
items.caption: Save More Tomorrow: commit part of each future raise to savings before you ever see it. At the first company that tried it, participants' average savings rate went from 3.5% to 13.6% in 40 months (Thaler & Benartzi, 2004). Educational, not personal advice.

titles: The One Sentence That Makes You Follow Through
If-Then Plans: The Science of Following Through
Stop Relying on Motivation. Use This Instead.
items.hook: One sentence makes you more likely to follow through on a goal.
items.caption: If-then plans ("implementation intentions"): a 2006 analysis of 94 studies by Gollwitzer and Sheeran found a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals. Write yours in the comments.
items.cta: Write your if-then sentence in the comments.

items.music: Soft focus beat; brief silence after "94 studies".

scenes.visual: Two puzzle pieces labeled IF and THEN clicking together

scenes.narration: Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer named it an implementation intention.

titles: Why We Trust Machines That Talk Back
items.hook: In the 1960s, a program felt so real its creator's secretary asked him to leave the room.
items.caption: ELIZA, built by MIT's Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s, only matched patterns, yet people confided in it anyway. The lesson still applies to every chatbot: fluent isn't the same as correct.
items.cta: Follow for the true stories behind the tech you use every day.

thumbnail.prompt: Vintage 1960s computer terminal glowing green text in a dim office, empty chair in front of it, cinematic, vertical 9:16, empty space at top for text

items.voice: Measured documentary narrator, about 155 words per minute; quiet pause after "leave the room".
items.music: Retro synth pad, slow and slightly eerie; lifts gently for the takeaway.

scenes.narration: In the 1960s, a program felt so real its creator's secretary asked him to leave the room.
scenes.visual: Vintage computer terminal with green text in a dim 1960s office

scenes.narration: The program was ELIZA, written by MIT professor Joseph Weizenbaum.
scenes.visual: Old university hallway with wood doors, 1960s feel, no people

scenes.visual: Hands resting on a vintage keyboard, hesitating

scenes.narration: It unsettled him so much that he became one of AI's sharpest early critics.
scenes.visual: Stack of typed manuscript pages on a desk under a lamp

scenes.narration: The reaction now has a name: the ELIZA effect.
scenes.visual: Bold white title text appearing on a black background

scenes.narration: We read understanding into anything that talks back fluently.
scenes.visual: Modern phone screen with a chat bubble interface, generic design

scenes.visual: Chat bubble with a red underline appearing beneath one sentence

scenes.visual: Magnifying glass moving over printed text

scenes.narration: Because a smooth talker was fooling people back in the 1960s too.

items.loopLine: Because a smooth talker was fooling people back in the 1960s too.
factCheck: ELIZA was created by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT and described in a 1966 paper
Its best-known script, DOCTOR, imitated a Rogerian psychotherapist by reflecting users' statements back as questions
Weizenbaum wrote in Computer Power and Human Reason (1976) that his secretary, who had watched him work on the program for months, asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it
Weizenbaum became a prominent critic of over-trusting computers
The term "ELIZA effect" describes people attributing understanding to computer programs
